title: Northwest Pipeline at 70: Built on reliability, ready for what’s next
summary: For generations, Northwest Pipeline has helped deliver natural gas when and where the West depends on it, and Williams is investing to keep the system ready for the future.
body_text: Key highlights Northwest Pipeline marks 70 years of dependable natural gas service across the West. Williams is investing in expansions and modernization to meet growing regional energy demand. Employees and customers are helping shape the system’s next era of reliability and growth. As Northwest Pipeline marks 70 years, Williams is building on decades of dependable natural gas service, with experienced employees and an expansion strategy focused on meeting the West’s energy needs for years to come. Northwest Pipeline’s roots trace to the mid-1950s, when Pacific Northwest Pipeline Corp. built a 1,500-mile line linking San Juan Basin gas to growing markets in the Pacific Northwest. The project was memorialized in the 1956 short film “ The Scenic Inch ,” a nod to the terrain and communities the line would cross. Today, that backbone has grown into a nearly 4,000-mile, bidirectional transmission network spanning six Western states, with 41 compressor stations, approximately 3.8 million dekatherms per day of peak design capacity and seasonal storage to help manage winter demand and supply disruptions. Reliability when the West needs it most Northwest Pipeline’s geographic footprint, strong customer relationships, storage connectivity and operating strength help Williams connect energy supply with growing demand across the West. Gary Venz, director of commercial services for Northwest Pipeline That role is becoming even more important as the region adds electric load, retires coal generation and depends on natural gas to support reliability when renewable output is constrained. The Northwest Gas Association says natural gas provides nearly three-quarters of the region’s energy use during extreme weather events, while the Northwest Power and Conservation Council has identified data centers as an emerging source of future power needs. Those trends show why the West needs infrastructure that can respond on the coldest days, support the grid during peak conditions and keep energy affordable and available. Meeting that demand depends not only on steel, compressors and storage, but on the people who know the system mile by mile. One of Northwest Pipeline’s most notable engineering projects is its Flaming Gorge crossing in Wyoming. Built after Flaming Gorge Dam required the pipeline to be rerouted, the 1962 suspension bridge holds the pipeline nearly 350 feet above the Green River and reservoir, with a 1,919-foot main span. More than six decades later, it remains a visible example of the innovation that helped Northwest Pipeline grow across the West. People behind dependable service Across compressor stations, control rooms, field operations and commercial teams, employees help Northwest Pipeline operate safely and efficiently while delivering dependable service to customers and communities. Technical specialist Lynn Stoll has worked on Northwest Pipeline for nearly 45 years, the second of three generations of Stolls working for Williams. From his Washam, Wyoming, home, he can see both the Flaming Gorge pipeline crossing — an engineering feat of the early 1960s — and the construction site of a new compressor station. The views connect the pipeline’s past and future, reflecting a system that continues to support the region’s economy, safety and growth. “We’ve always been part of the community out here,” Stoll said, “providing good jobs, working closely with emergency responders and helping where we can. But the biggest change has been safety. We build smarter, inspect more closely and maintain the system better, with stronger tools and standards than we had decades ago. When you look at where it started and where it is now, it’s pretty remarkable.” Rob Harmon, operations director for Williams’ Pacific division, started as an engineering intern at Northwest Pipeline in the early 1990s. “I remember being very impressed with the culture,” he said. “The camaraderie, teamwork and willingness to share knowledge was evident from day one. Even all these years later, the people and the culture are still what stands out and makes us excel.” Investing for the next era Williams is building on that legacy with a phased expansion strategy to help meet growing demand across the West. Projects such as Wild Trail, Stanfield South, the Naughton Coal-to-Gas Conversion Project and Silver Spur are expanding market access, enhancing reliability, supporting power generation and creating new opportunities for customers. For director of projects Jeremiah Ross, who has spent 24 years at Williams, the growth underway on Northwest Pipeline reflects more than new infrastructure. It reflects a strong culture among the employees who operate, maintain and expand the system — people who take ownership in building projects that matter. “We’re in a very exciting period for Northwest Pipeline,” Ross said. “The demand for energy and electricity in the region is creating opportunities to expand the system, serve more customers and build the next generation of projects that will support growth across the West.” Pacific Northwest Pipeline’s History 1956: Pacific Northwest Pipeline completes the original 1,500-mile system, memorialized in the film “The Scenic Inch.” 1957: El Paso Natural Gas acquires Pacific Northwest Pipeline 1960s: The system expands with the region’s growing homes, businesses and industry . 1970s: Additional upgrades strengthen service across the West. 1983: Williams acquires Northwest Energy Company, adding to its interstate pipeline network. 1990s: Modernization projects improve flexibility and operating efficiency. 2010s: Transported volumes rise as the system supports regional energy reliability. 2023: Williams highlights more than 65 years of expansion, maintenance and inspection. 2025: Projects including Kelso Beaver and Wild Trail advance to support future demand. 2026 and beyond: Silver Spur and other upgrades help prepare for the next era of growth. Growth is only one part of the investment story. Williams also is advancing one of the most significant modernization efforts in Northwest Pipeline’s history. Through the Emissions Reduction Program and broader system upgrades, the company is replacing legacy infrastructure with modern, lower-emission technologies that improve efficiency, strengthen reliability and enhance operational flexibility. Together with customers, Williams is investing in safe, resilient infrastructure to support the region’s changing energy needs. After 70 years of fueling homes, businesses and communities across the West, Northwest Pipeline is entering its next chapter with the same priorities that built its first: safe operations, dependable service and room to grow.

title: Where Do Skills Go on a Resume? The Skills-Section Debate
summary: Do you even need a skills section? Where it goes, hard vs soft skills, whether the ATS reads it, and a clean format that works. The structure debate, settled.
body_text: Do you even need a skills section on your resume? Usually yes, but for two narrow reasons: it's the block a recruiter's keyword search actually reads, and it's a fast index of your hard skills. That's it. It is not a place to list soft-skill adjectives. Where it goes depends on whether your skills are the pitch. A career-changer puts it up top. A senior engineer with proof in every bullet can drop it to a compact strip lower down. Fill it with concrete, defensible hard skills that mirror the job posting, and prove the rest in your experience. Ask ten people where skills go on a resume and you'll get ten answers, half of them contradicting the other half. Put it at the top. No, bury it at the bottom. List everything you know. No, list only what the job asks for. Use a section. Skip the section and weave skills into your bullets. It's genuinely confusing, and most of the advice floating around treats the skills section like a checkbox instead of what it really is: a small piece of prime real estate that does one or two specific jobs, and does nothing at all if you fill it wrong. So let's settle it. Not with a list of 100 skills to include (that's a different question, and there's a whole guide on which skills to put on a resume for that). This is about structure. Do you need the section, where does it belong, what actually goes in it, and does the software even read it. What a skills section is actually for A skills section earns its space for exactly two reasons. Both are worth understanding, because once you know them, every other decision gets easier. The first is search. When a recruiter opens a req with 400 applicants, they don't read 400 resumes front to back. They can't. What they often do instead is run a search inside the applicant tracking system or on LinkedIn Recruiter, looking for the specific terms the role needs. Something like Java combined with a few framework names, a database or two, maybe a cloud platform. The people whose resumes contain those exact words surface. The people who wrote around them, or used a different word for the same thing, sink. Your skills section is where those searchable terms live in one dense, easy-to-index place. It's the part of your resume built for a keyword query. The second reason is the human glance. Recruiters and hiring managers spend very little time on a first pass, and most of that time lands on the top third of the first page. A hiring manager scanning a stack wants to confirm the stack fast: does this person have the tools, the languages, the certifications this role runs on. A tight skills section answers that in one look, without making anyone dig through three jobs of bullet points to reconstruct your toolkit. (More on that quick pass in our breakdown of how long recruiters actually spend on a resume .) That's the whole case for the section. Searchable real estate, plus a fast index. Notice what's not on the list: it is not a personality summary, not a place to prove you're a team player, and definitely not a spot to pad your resume so it looks fuller. Every skills section that fails does so because it forgot those two jobs and tried to do a third one. Do you really need one at all? For most people, keep it. The two jobs above are real, and a compact skills section handles them cheaply. But "keep it" doesn't mean "give it a quarter of the page." The size and position should match how much work the section is doing for you. There's one honest exception worth naming. If you're a senior person whose skills are already obvious from what you've built, the section stops carrying much weight. When your most recent bullet says you migrated a monolith to microservices on AWS, nobody needs a separate line telling them you know AWS. In that case the section becomes a quick reference strip, not a headline. You keep it because the ATS search still reads it, but you don't let it crowd out the experience that's actually selling you. The people who genuinely lean on the section are the ones whose experience doesn't tell the whole story yet. New grads. Career-changers. Anyone whose job titles don't advertise the skills they actually have. For them the section isn't filler, it's the pitch, and it deserves room near the top. So the real answer to "do I need one" is less about a rule and more about a question: are my skills doing the selling here, or is my experience? Where it goes: top or bottom is a decision, not a rule Here's where most advice goes wrong. It hands you a fixed position ("skills always go under the summary" or "skills always go at the bottom") as if resumes were interchangeable. They're not. Placement is a decision you make based on one thing: whether your skills are your strongest selling point. Put the section high, right under your summary or header, when your skills are the pitch. That's the career-changer moving from teaching into project coordination, the bootcamp grad with a real stack but a thin work history, the specialist whose value is a specific technical toolkit. These readers need to see the toolset before they get to experience that looks unrelated or light. If a hiring manager glances at the top third and sees the exact competencies the role needs, you've bought yourself the extra thirty seconds it takes to earn a real read. Drop the section lower, as a compact strip, when your experience is the pitch. A senior engineer with eight years of proof in the bullets doesn't lead with a skills list. The recent roles do the heavy lifting, and the section sits underneath as a fast index for anyone (or any search) that wants to confirm the toolkit. It's still there. It's just not taking the spot that your best accomplishment should own. The principle underneath both cases is the same. Whatever earns you the interview goes where the eye lands first. For a changer, that's the skills. For a proven senior IC, that's the most recent role. Match the layout to the argument you're making, and the top-versus-bottom debate answers itself. Hard skills belong here. Soft skills mostly don't. This is the single most useful distinction in the whole debate, and it's the one people get wrong most often. Hard skills belong in the section. Languages, frameworks, tools, platforms, certifications, software, technical methods. These are concrete and verifiable in a way soft skills never are, and, critically, they're the terms a recruiter searches for. "Python," "Salesforce," "AutoCAD," "SOC 2," "SQL," "Adobe Premiere." A reader can look at these and know exactly what you can do, and a search can find them. This is what the section is built to hold. A list of soft skills is a different animal, and as a list it's close to worthless. "Communication, teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, detail-oriented, quick learner." Nobody reads those and believes them, because everybody writes them. Anyone can type "excellent communication skills" whether it's true or not, so the words carry no signal. Recruiters have said this plainly for years: a self-asserted soft skill in a list means nothing. It's the resume equivalent of a stranger telling you they're trustworthy. That doesn't mean soft skills don't matter. They matter enormously. It means they don't belong in a list. You prove a soft skill by showing it in action, tied to a hard skill and a result. Not "leadership" in a section, but a bullet that says you led a team of four through a system migration and cut processing time. Not "communication" as a word, but a line about translating requirements from stakeholders into something engineering could ship. The soft skill lives inside the accomplishment, where it's believable, and we go deeper on that move in the guide to proving achievements even when you don't have numbers . If you must reference soft skills directly for a role that explicitly asks, weave in only the ones the posting names, and back each one somewhere in your experience. There's more on choosing between the two in our rundowns of hard skills for a resume and soft skills on a resume . Does the ATS actually read the skills section? Yes, and this is where the section really earns its keep, but the way it gets read is different from the scare stories. The applicant tracking system isn't sitting there auto-rejecting you because your skills section is missing a magic word. That's a myth we've taken apart before in detail (see the ATS auto-reject myth ). What actually happens is closer to a database query. Recruiters search the pool for candidates who match the role, and the skills section is one of the richest places those searches land. On LinkedIn Recruiter, for instance, a term you've added to your Skills list can surface your profile even if that word appears nowhere else. The section is, quite literally, indexed and searchable. Which leads to the one move that matters: mirror the job description's real terms. If the posting says "PostgreSQL," write "PostgreSQL," not just "SQL." If it says "Kubernetes," don't leave it at "container orchestration." Recruiters search for the specific tokens the hiring manager gave them, and a synonym you assume is obvious might not be the word being typed into the search box. Use the exact language the role uses, for the skills you genuinely have. Before you send anything, it's worth checking that your skills section is mirroring the posting's real terms and that a parser can actually read it. A quick free resume review flags the gaps in seconds, which beats guessing. Is your skills section pulling its weight? See whether your skills mirror the job's real keywords and whether a parser reads them cleanly, before a recruiter ever does. Run a free resume review → Mirroring the job description vs. stuffing it There's a line between using the job's real vocabulary and gaming the system, and it's worth being clear about where it sits, because crossing it hurts you. Mirroring is honest. You read the posting, you find the skills you actually have that it names, and you use its exact words for them. You're not adding anything false. You're making sure the terms you legitimately own are findable. That's smart, and it's what recruiters expect a serious applicant to do. Stuffing is the opposite instinct taken too far. It's the 40-item everything-list, the block of buzzwords you half-remember from a tutorial, the skills you crammed in because they showed up in the posting even though you've never touched them. It's also the old white-text trick, where people paste keywords in a color that blends into the page, which parsers and recruiters caught onto a long time ago (we buried that one in the piece on the white-text resume hack ). Stuffing backfires two ways. It dilutes your real signal, so the skills that matter get lost in noise. And the moment a recruiter reads the section, or you sit down in an interview, the padding is obvious, and it costs you trust. The trouble really starts with the word "keywords" itself, which makes it sound like there are magic phrases that unlock the pile. There aren't. What matters is whether your resume shows you can do the job. If a company is hiring a WordPress developer, they look for real WordPress experience, not the word dropped into a list. That's it. Section vs. woven into experience: it's both People frame this as an either/or. Do I put skills in a section, or do I work them into my job bullets? The answer is you do both, because the two placements aren't competing. They're doing different jobs. The section is your index. It's scannable, it's searchable, and it lets a reader or a query confirm your toolkit in a second. The bullets are your proof. That's where a skill stops being a claim and becomes something you clearly did, in context, with a result attached. A skill that shows up only in the section and never once in your experience is a red flag waiting to happen. It reads as a word you added rather than a thing you've done, and any interviewer worth their salt will poke at exactly those items. So the healthy pattern is simple. Your most important skills appear in both places. The section lists them so you surface and scan well. The bullets demonstrate them so the claim holds up. Don't make the recruiter or the ATS choose between an index and a proof when you can give them both. The everything-list trap The most common way a skills section goes wrong is length. Someone decides that if a few keywords help, forty must help more, and the section balloons into a wall of comma-separated terms covering every piece of software they've ever opened. It doesn't work, and it actively hurts. A 40-skill list tells a recruiter nothing, because it's not a set of priorities, it's a data dump. When everything is listed, nothing is emphasized, and the real, role-critical skills get buried among the filler. Worse, it reads as spam. A hiring manager who sees "Microsoft Word, email, teamwork, Google, communication, time management" alongside your actual technical stack starts to distrust the whole section. The fix is discipline. Somewhere in the range of eight to fifteen focused hard skills, chosen for this role, beats forty every time. Cut anything you couldn't discuss for five minutes in an interview. Cut the skills so basic they're assumed (nobody's impressed you can use email). Cut the ones that have nothing to do with the job you're targeting. A short, sharp, relevant section signals judgment. A long one signals that you couldn't decide what mattered. Don't list skills you can't defend Here's a filter that quietly solves a lot of problems: everything in your skills section is fair game in the interview. If you put it there, you're inviting a question about it. This is why self-ratings are a trap. Give yourself "Python: 5/5" and you've painted a target on your own resume. Any competent interviewer will aim their hardest question straight at your self-declared five, because that's where you told them you were strongest, and if you fold under it, the gap between your rating and your reality is now the story. The same logic applies to any skill you inflated. List "advanced Excel" when you can build a pivot table but freeze at an INDEX-MATCH, and you're one question away from an awkward pause. So run every line through one test: could I hold a real conversation about this with someone who knows the field? If yes, it belongs. If it's aspirational, something you're learning or touched once, either leave it off or represent it honestly. A skills section full of things you can actually back up is a section that helps you in the room. One padded with claims you can't defend is a liability you're carrying into every interview. Skill bars, columns, and other formatting mistakes Even a well-chosen skills section can be sabotaged by how it's laid out. Two formatting habits do the most damage. The first is visual skill ratings: the bars, the dots, the little charts showing you're "80% proficient" in Excel. They look polished and they communicate nothing. A bar that's three-quarters full next to a tool tells a reader nothing about what you can actually do with it, and it eats space that a real accomplishment could use. It also runs straight into the self-rating problem above, handing an interviewer a number to attack. We made the full case against them in the piece on skill bars on a resume , and the short version is: drop them. Plain text beats a graphic every time. The second is layout that breaks parsing. Multi-column skill grids, text tucked inside graphics, icons standing in for words. These can look clean to a human and turn to garbage when a parser tries to read them, scrambling the order or dropping the terms entirely. If you want to confirm your section survives the software, you can run the plain checks in our guide on how to test whether your resume is ATS-friendly . Keep the section single-column, plain text, real characters. Boring parses. Fancy fails. A clean skills-section format that works Strip away the debate and the actual spec is short. Here's what a skills section should look like when it's doing its two jobs and nothing else. Group your skills into a few labeled categories so a human parses them instantly. For a developer that might be Languages, then Frameworks, then Tools, then Cloud and data. For an analyst it might be Software, then Technical, then Certifications. The grouping does two things: it makes the section scannable, and it quietly signals that you understand how your own field organizes its tools. Under each label, list plain comma-separated terms. No bars, no dots, no percentages, no self-ratings, no icons. Give the section a plain, real heading. "Skills," "Technical Skills," "Core Competencies," or "Areas of Expertise" all parse fine and all read fine. Keep the whole thing to roughly eight to fifteen defensible hard skills, tuned to the specific job you're applying to, using the posting's exact vocabulary for the skills you genuinely have. Single column. Plain text. That's the entire recipe. It's not clever, and it's not supposed to be. A skills section is a fast index and a searchable block, and the cleanest version of it wins. If you get this piece right and your resume is still stalling, the problem is probably somewhere else on the page. Our recruiter-POV teardown of why a resume keeps getting rejected walks the rest of it, and the full breakdown of how hiring actually works shows where your resume sits in the whole process, from the first search to the offer. Frequently Asked Questions Where should the skills section go, top or bottom? Depends on one thing: are your skills the pitch, or is your experience? A career-changer or a new grad with a real stack but a thin work history wants that section high, right under the summary, so the toolkit shows before the light experience does. A senior person with proof in every bullet can push it down to a small strip. Lead with whatever gets you the interview. Should I list soft skills like communication and teamwork? Not as a list, no. The moment you type "great communicator, team player, quick learner," you've written what everyone writes, and a reader discounts it on sight. Soft skills earn belief only when you show them working. So instead of a "leadership" line, write the bullet about the four-person migration you ran. If a posting names a specific soft skill, back that one inside your experience rather than parking the word in a section. Does the ATS actually read my skills section? It does, and this is where the section pays off. Recruiters search the applicant pool for the exact terms a role needs, and your skills block is one of the densest, most findable places those terms sit. On LinkedIn Recruiter a skill you've added can surface you even when the word appears nowhere else. What it does not do is auto-reject you for a missing word. It sorts and finds. It doesn't slam a door. How many skills should I list? Somewhere around eight to fifteen, all defensible, all tuned to the job in front of you. Forty is a data dump that buries the three skills that actually matter and reads like spam to anyone who's screened a stack of resumes. Drop the ones you couldn't talk about for five minutes. Drop the ones so basic they're assumed, like email. What's left is a section that signals judgment. What's the difference between mirroring a job description and keyword stuffing? Mirroring is honest borrowing. You read the posting, spot the skills you genuinely have, and use its exact words for them, so your real qualifications turn up in a search. Stuffing is padding: forty buzzwords, terms you've never touched, keywords crammed in because they appeared in the ad. One helps you surface. The other dilutes your real signal and falls apart the second a recruiter or an interviewer looks closely. Should skills go in a section or inside my experience bullets? Both, and they're not competing. Think of the section as the index and the bullets as the proof. The index is scannable and searchable; the proof is where a skill sits in context with a result attached and stops being a bare claim. Your most important skills should show up in both. A skill that appears only in the section and never once in your experience is exactly the line an interviewer circles. Are skill bars, dots, or percentage ratings a good idea? Skip them. A bar that's three-quarters full next to a tool looks tidy and says nothing about what you can build with it. Worse, it hands an interviewer a self-rating to aim at. Mark yourself five out of five on something and watch the hardest question of the day land right there. Plain words do the job that a graphic can't. What should I actually name the section? Keep the heading boring. "Skills," "Technical Skills," "Core Competencies," and "Areas of Expertise" all parse cleanly and read clearly to a human. The only trap here is getting clever with a stylized or graphic label a parser might miss entirely. The heading has one job, which is telling a person and a machine that your hard skills follow. Let it do that and move on. Which specific skills should I choose to list? Pick the hard skills the target job names that you can genuinely back up, using the posting's exact terms. It's a role-by-role call, not one fixed list you reuse forever. For examples broken out by field and category, the guide on which skills to put on a resume covers the specifics. This piece stays deliberately on the structure and placement around them. Can I just skip the skills section entirely? You can. You probably shouldn't. Cutting it removes the searchable block recruiters actually query and forces a human to piece your toolkit together from your bullets. Even a proven senior candidate tends to keep a compact strip so the search still finds the right terms. It costs almost nothing to keep and quite a lot to lose, so shrink it before you ever reach for the delete key. title: Natural Gas Services Group, Inc. Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial and Operating Results; Announces Dividend and Provides Updated Guidance
summary: SOUTHLAKE, Texas, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Natural Gas Services Group, Inc. (“NGS” or the “Company”) (NYSE:NGS), a leading provider of natural gas compression equipment, technology, and services to the energy industry, today announced financial results for the three months ended June 30,
body_text: SOUTHLAKE, Texas, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Natural Gas Services Group, Inc. (“NGS” or the “Company”) (NYSE:NGS), a leading provider of natural gas compression equipment, technology, and services to the energy industry, today announced financial results for the three months ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Rental revenue of $49.4 million for the second quarter of 2026 represents a 24.9% year-over-year increase and a 4.9% sequential increase compared to the first quarter of 2026. Net income of $3.8 million, or $0.30 per diluted share, for the second quarter of 2026 compared to $5.2 million or $0.41 per diluted share for the second quarter of 2025 and $6.8 million, or $0.53 per diluted share for the first quarter of 2026. Adjusted Net Income(1) for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $6.1 million, or $0.47 per diluted share, compared to Adjusted Net Income of $5.3 million, or $0.42 per diluted share, for the comparable 2025 period. Completed the acquisition of Flatrock Compression Holdings, LLC ("Flatrock") on June 12, 2026, adding 87,233 rented horsepower (the "Flatrock Acquisition"). Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $25.1 million for the second quarter of 2026, represents a 27.4% year-over-year increase and a 3.3% increase sequentially. Returned $1.9 million to shareholders during the second quarter of 2026 through the Company's quarterly dividend of $0.15 per share and announced a third-quarter dividend of $0.15 per share to stockholders of record as of August 19, 2026, expected to be paid on September 2, 2026. Management Commentary and Outlook "NGS delivered a record second quarter and a milestone first half of 2026," said Justin Jacobs, Chief Executive Officer. "Second quarter rental revenue increased 25% year over year, Adjusted EBITDA increased 27% year over year, and horsepower utilization reached a record 88.3%. These results reflect great field execution and strong demand for our fleet." "The acquisition of Flatrock added approximately 92,600 total horsepower to our fleet, improved our unit density in key growth basins, and accelerated our electric motor drive strategy. With only a partial month of Flatrock results included in the quarter, the full financial benefit of the combined platform remains ahead of us. Integration is progressing well, and we already see meaningful opportunities to diversify organic growth, improve field operating efficiency, and enhance fixed cost leverage." "Organic momentum also remains strong. We added 22,200 total horsepower during the first half of 2026, with large horsepower electric motor drive equipment comprising well more than half of those additions, and we now expect to deploy at least 55,000 horsepower organically this year. Industry fundamentals remain constructive, supported by high utilization, constrained equipment supply, and growing compression requirements tied to oil and gas production, LNG exports, and power demand." "Based on our record first-half performance and the Flatrock Acquisition, we are increasing full-year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $103 million to $108 million. We ended the quarter with bank covenant leverage of 2.77x and more than $170 million of facility capacity providing flexibility to continue executing our strategic growth levers while returning capital to shareholders." (1) For a definition of Adjusted Gross Margin, Adjusted Net Income and Adjusted EBITDA and reconciliation to their most directly comparable financial measures calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP, please see “Non-GAAP Financial Measures - Adjusted Gross Margin,” “Non-GAAP Financial Measures - Adjusted Net Income” and “Non-GAAP Financial Measures - Adjusted EBITDA” below. Corporate Guidance — 2026 Outlook The Company now expects 2026 Adjusted EBITDA of $103 million to $108 million, compared to prior guidance of $92.5 million to $97.5 million. The updated guidance reflects record first-half performance, the June 12 acquisition of Flatrock, high utilization, and contracted organic fleet expansion balanced with expected inflationary pressures during the remainder of 2026. Outlook FY 2026 Adjusted EBITDA $103 million - $108 million FY 2026 Growth Capital Expenditures $60 million - $80 million FY 2026 Maintenance Capital Expenditures $15 million - $19 million The outlook for capital expenditures has been updated to reflect the larger combined fleet and growth commitments following the acquisition of Flatrock. Growth capital expenditures for 2026 are expected in the range of $60 million to $80 million, excluding acquisition consideration, and remain focused on the deployment of large horsepower and electric motor drive compression units. Maintenance capital expenditures for 2026 are expected in the range of $15 million to $19 million. Consistent with prior periods, the Company remains committed to disciplined capital allocation and investing in assets that generate attractive long-term returns. The Company's operating cash flow, expanded $500 million credit facility, and significant borrowing capacity provide flexibility to integrate Flatrock, fund organic growth, pursue accretive acquisitions, and return capital to shareholders. 2026 Second Quarter Financial Results Revenue : Total revenue for the three months ended June 30, 2026, increased 24.2% to $51.4 million from $41.4 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025. This increase was primarily attributable to higher rental revenues for the comparable periods. Rental revenue increased 24.9% to $49.4 million from $39.6 million in the second quarter of 2025 driven by contracted fleet expansion and continued pricing strength across the company's fleet. Revenues provided by Flatrock during the partial month period were $2.2 million. As of June 30, 2026, we had 669,919 rented horsepower (1,521 utilized units) compared to 498,651 horsepower (1,198 utilized units) as of June 30, 2025, reflecting a 34.3% increase in total utilized horsepower. Flatrock accounted for 87,233 rented horsepower from 270 utilized units. Gross Margins and Adjusted Gross Margins (1) : Total gross margins, including depreciation expense increased to $20.1 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to $15.4 million for the same period in 2025. Total Adjusted Gross Margin, exclusive of depreciation expense, increased to $30.8 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to $24.2 million for the same period in 2025. Operating Income: Operating income for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $9.9 million and was essentially unchanged from the comparable 2025 period. Net Income and Adjusted Net Income (1) : Net income for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $3.8 million, or $0.30 per diluted share, compared to net income of $5.2 million, or $0.41 per diluted share, for the comparable 2025 period and $6.8 million, or $0.53 per diluted share for the three months ended March 31, 2026. The year-over-year and sequential decline in net income were driven by $3.3 million of strategic transaction costs attributable to the Flatrock Acquisition embedded in selling, general and administrative expenses, partially offset by increases in rental revenue and the associated gross margin impact. Adjusted Net Income for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $6.1 million, or $0.47 per diluted share, compared to Adjusted Net Income of $5.3 million, or $0.42 per diluted share, for the comparable 2025 period. Cash Flows: For the three months ended June 30, 2026, cash flows provided by operating activities were $25.4 million, while cash flows used in investing activities were $127.5 million which includes $108.7 million for the cash portion of the Flatrock Acquisition, net of cash acquired and $18.8 million of capital expenditures including $15.4 million and $3.4 million for growth and maintenance, respectively. This compares to cash flows from operating activities of $11.0 million and cash flows used in investing activities of $25.7 million for the comparable period in 2025. Adjusted EBITDA (1) : Adjusted EBITDA increased 27.4% to $25.1 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, from $19.7 million for the same period in 2025. The increase was primarily attributable to higher rental revenue and rental adjusted gross margin. Sequentially, Adjusted EBITDA increased 3.3% when compared to $24.3 million for the three months ended March 31, 2026. Debt: Outstanding debt on our revolving credit facility as of June 30, 2026, was $328.0 million with over $170 million available on our facility and $134.8 million of availability, reflecting the applicable borrowing base calculation. Our leverage ratio as of June 30, 2026, was 2.77x and our fixed charge coverage ratio was 4.18x. As of June 30, 2026, the Company was in compliance with all terms, conditions and covenants of the credit agreement. Adjusted gross margin is the difference between revenue and cost of sales, exclusive of depreciation. Adjusted Net income: “Adjusted Net Income” is a non-GAAP financial measure that we define as net income (loss) adjusted for nonrecurring interest income attributable to income tax refunds, impairments, nonrecurring restructuring charges including severance and costs directly attributable to strategic transactions, including the Flatrock Acquisition, and income tax effects of these adjustments. We believe that Adjusted Net Income and Adjusted Net Income per share amounts provide meaningful supplemental information regarding our operational performance on a recurring basis. Adjusted Gross Margin is included as a supplemental disclosure because it is a primary measure used by our management as it represents the results of revenue and costs (excluding depreciation and amortization expense), which are key components of our operations. Adjusted Gross Margin differs from gross margin, in that gross margin includes depreciation and amortization expense. We believe Adjusted Gross Margin is important because it focuses on the current operating performance of our operations and excludes the impact of the prior historical costs of the assets acquired or constructed that are utilized in those operations. Depreciation and amortization expense does not accurately reflect the costs required to maintain and replenish the operational usage of our assets and therefore may not portray the costs from current operating activity. Rather, depreciation and amortization expense reflects the systematic allocation of historical property and equipment costs over their estimated useful lives. Adjusted Gross Margin has certain material limitations associated with its use as compared to gross margin. These limitations are primarily due to the exclusion of depreciation and amortization expense, which is material to our results of operations. Because we use capital assets, depreciation and amortization expense is a necessary element of our costs and our ability to generate revenue. In order to compensate for these limitations, management uses this non-GAAP measure as a supplemental measure to other GAAP results to provide a more complete understanding of our performance. As an indicator of our operating performance, Adjusted Gross Margin should not be considered an alternative to, or more meaningful than, gross margin as determined in accordance with GAAP. Our Adjusted Gross Margin may not be comparable to a similarly titled measure of another company because other entities may not calculate Adjusted Gross Margin in the same manner. This term, as used and defined by us, may not be comparable to similarly titled measures employed by other companies and is not a measure of performance calculated in accordance with GAAP. Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for operating income, net income or loss, cash flows provided by operating, investing and financing activities, or other income or cash flow statement data prepared in accordance with GAAP. However, management believes Adjusted EBITDA is useful to an investor in evaluating our operating performance because: (i) it is widely used by investors in the energy industry to measure a company’s operating performance without regard to items excluded from the calculation of Adjusted EBITDA, which can vary substantially from company to company depending upon accounting methods and book value of assets, capital structure and the method by which assets were acquired, among other factors; (ii) it helps investors to more meaningfully evaluate and compare the results of our operations from period to period by removing the impact of our capital structure and asset base from our operating structure; and (iii) it is used by our management for various purposes, including as a measure of operating performance, in presentations to our Board of Directors, and as a basis for strategic planning and forecasting. Adjusted EBITDA has limitations as an analytical tool, and you should not consider it in isolation, or as a substitute for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Some of these limitations are as follows: (i) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect all our cash expenditures, future requirements for capital expenditures, or contractual commitments; (ii) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect changes in, or cash requirements for, our working capital needs; (iii) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect the cash requirements necessary to service interest or principal payments on our debt and finance leases; and (iv) although depreciation and amortization are non-cash charges, the assets being depreciated and amortized will often have to be replaced in the future, and Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect any capital expenditures for such replacements. summary: BOSTON, Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- X4 Pharmaceuticals (Nasdaq: XFOR), a company focused on improving the lives of people with rare hematology diseases, today announced that, effective on July 31, 2026, the company issued inducement awards to new employees under the X4 Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
body_text: X4 Pharmaceuticals Announces Inducement Grants Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4) August 3, 2026 PDF Version BOSTON, Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- X4 Pharmaceuticals (Nasdaq: XFOR), a company focused on improving the lives of people with rare hematology diseases, today announced that, effective on July 31, 2026, the company issued inducement awards to new employees under the X4 Pharmaceuticals, Inc. 2019 Inducement Equity Incentive Plan (the “2019 Inducement Plan”). The 2019 Inducement Plan is used exclusively for the grant of equity awards to individuals who were not previously an employee of X4. The inducement awards consist of options to purchase an aggregate of 12,000 shares of X4’s common stock. These stock awards were granted as an inducement material to the new employees entering into employment with X4 in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4) and were approved by X4’s Compensation Committee of the Board of Directors. The options have a ten-year term and an exercise price of $3.98 per share, which is equal to the closing price of X4’s common stock on July 31, 2026. Each option will vest over a four-year period, with 25% of the shares vesting after 12 months and the remaining shares vesting monthly over the following 36 months, subject to the employee’s continued employment with X4 on such vesting dates. The options are subject to the terms and conditions of the 2019 Inducement Plan and the terms and conditions of an award agreement covering the grant. About X4 Pharmaceuticals X4 Pharmaceuticals is a company focused on improving the lives of people with rare hematology diseases by developing and commercializing innovative therapies in areas with significant unmet needs. Leveraging expertise in diseases of the immune system and CXCR4 biology, X4 has successfully developed mavorixafor, an orally available CXCR4 antagonist that is approved in the U.S. and EU as XOLREMDI® for patients with WHIM syndrome. The Company is currently conducting a global, pivotal Phase 3 clinical trial (4WARD) evaluating mavorixafor in chronic neutropenic disorders. The U.S. FDA has granted Fast Track designation to mavorixafor for the treatment of chronic neutropenia. X4 is headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts. For more information, please visit www.x4pharma.com . X4 Investor Contact: Remy Bernarda Jenny Kobin IR Advisory Solutions ir@x4pharma.com Source: X4 Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

body_text: IREN Delivers Horizon 1 to Microsoft and Achieves NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud Status on GB300 NVL72 IREN Delivers Horizon 1 to Microsoft 133.8 KB NEW YORK, Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- IREN Limited (NASDAQ: IREN) (“IREN”) today announced that Horizon 1 has been delivered to and accepted by Microsoft, and that IREN has achieved NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud status on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72. Horizon 1 is the first of four 50MW (IT load) direct-to-chip liquid cooled AI Cloud deployments scheduled for delivery to Microsoft at IREN’s Childress, Texas campus in 2026 under a five-year, $9.7bn cloud services contract announced in November 2025. The rapid delivery of Horizon 1 to Microsoft reflects the agility of IREN’s vertically integrated model, which provides end-to-end control across design, engineering and construction of the data centers supporting its GPU deployments. IREN’s Exemplar Cloud status was achieved following NVIDIA’s testing of its NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 deployment at Horizon 1. The designation demonstrates IREN’s ability to support demanding AI workloads with performance, reliability and scale. IREN continues to target a broader expansion to 480MW (gross) AI Cloud capacity in 2026 and 1.2GW (gross) AI Cloud capacity in 2027. Daniel Roberts, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of IREN, said: “Delivering Horizon 1 demonstrates the strength of our vertically integrated model and our ability to execute complex AI infrastructure projects at speed and scale. I want to congratulate and thank the more than 3,000 people across our site team whose expertise, commitment and execution made this milestone possible. We look forward to building on this momentum with Microsoft as we work to deliver Horizons 2-4 later this year.” About IREN IREN is a vertically integrated AI Cloud platform, delivering data centers, compute and software for AI training and inference.
